name: Arasaleeswarar Temple, Thiru Arasili
deity: Shiva as Arasaleeswarar (Arasilinathar), the Lord of the arasu tree, with the goddess Periyanayaki
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Thondai Nadu, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century); medieval Chola inscriptions, with the present masonry largely of the later chieftains
dynasty: Medieval Cholas, with later rebuilding by regional chieftains
summary: Arasaleeswarar is the quiet Thondai Nadu shrine of Thiruvarasili, praised by Sambandar in the Tevaram, where Shiva is worshipped as a small self-manifested linga that first appeared to a sage beneath a sacred arasu, the peepal tree.

sections.history: Thiruvarasili lies in the Thondai Nadu, the land between the Palar and Pennai rivers, a short distance inland from the old coast near Puducherry. The temple is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines sung in the Tevaram, and the hymns of Sambandar praise its Lord. It is remembered in tradition as one of the Thondai Nadu temples in that sacred list. A handful of medieval inscriptions of the Chola period are recorded here, showing that the shrine was cared for and endowed in the centuries after the saints. The present stonework is believed to rest on an older Chola foundation and to have been raised largely in the sixteenth century by regional chieftains. The village is also called Ozhindiyapattu, a name that local belief reads as the place where what was lost was found again.
sections.architecture: The temple is a modest Dravidian complex of roughly two acres, entered beneath a three-tiered gopuram and ringed by a single enclosing prakaram. The sanctum holds Arasaleeswarar as a small swayambhu linga, said to be self-manifested rather than installed, and the worship is offered beneath a canopy of one hundred and eight rudraksha beads. The goddess Periyanayaki is honoured in her own separate shrine within the walls. The arasu, the peepal tree from which the Lord takes his name, is the sacred tree of the temple. Unlike the great towered shrines of the Kaveri plain, Arasili is intimate in scale, a village sanctuary whose beauty lies in its stillness rather than its height.
sections.legends: Two stories gather around the linga. In the first, the sage Vamadeva went from shrine to shrine in search of Shiva and, coming to this place, stood beneath an arasu tree in longing for the Lord's grace. Shiva appeared to him there as a self-manifested linga, and the tree gave the place and the deity their name. The second story concerns a childless king, Satyavardhana, who laid out a garden of flowers for the Lord, only to find the blossoms vanishing night after night. Resolved to catch the thief, he kept watch and saw a deer feeding in the garden. He loosed an arrow, and where it struck the tree a linga was found bleeding. Shiva revealed that the deer was none other than himself and blessed the king with children. Devotees say the mark of the arrow remains on the linga, and it is covered with cloth during worship.
sections.festivals: The great festival of Arasili is the ten-day Vaikasi Brahmotsavam in May and June, when the deities are carried in procession through the village. Maha Shivaratri in February or March and the lamp festival of Karthigai in November or December are kept with devotion, and the monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. The shrine is also held dear by those born under the Pushya (Poosam) star, who come to worship here. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Arasili is a temple for those who prefer stillness to spectacle. A branch road leads east from the main highway through quiet fields to the small gopuram, and inside there is little crowd and no hurry. Stand before the small linga beneath its canopy of rudraksha beads, look for the cloth that veils the old arrow mark, and then turn to Periyanayaki in her shrine. Sit a while under the sacred tree in the courtyard. There are few shops or eating places near the temple, so bring water and anything you need for worship, and combine the visit with other temples of the Puducherry and Tindivanam country.

visit.timings: Commonly open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon to evening, with a break in between; sources differ, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer courtyard but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is about 16 km from Puducherry, in the village of Ozhindiyapattu on the Puducherry–Kilianur–Tindivanam road. From the main road junction a branch road runs east for about 2 km to the temple. Kilianur and the Tevaram shrine of Irumbai Mahakalam are each around 8 km away. Buses serve the highway, but there are few shops or eateries near the temple, so a private vehicle from Puducherry is the easiest way to reach it.
